To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the steady-state slope of a river incised into bedrock by sediment transport can be predicted by the saltation– abrasion model, and that this model predicts that steady- state slope is most sensitive, in terms of the magnitude of the slope response, to changes in grain sizes, and least sensitive to changes in rock uplift rate.

(1) bedload saltation is the dominant process for bedrock incision by rivers, (2) the saltation-abrassion model predicts the steady-state channel slopes of rivers, and (3) sediment supply and grain size are more important than rock uplift rate and bedrock strength in determining the steady-state channel gradient of a bedrock river.

(a) bedrock river incision by saltating bed material is a threshold-controlled abrasion process, and (b) the steady-state channel gradient is most sensitive to the size distribution of bedload sediments, which may be controlled by the size distribution of sediment delivered to the channel network by hillslope sediment supply.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

a saltation–abrasive incision model that includes the threshold of grain movement and the cover effect is a good starting place for modeling bedrock river incision and that the threshold of grain mobility is the single most important sediment effect that should be included in incision models.

the saltation– abrasion model is a good starting point for predicting channel slope, but that it is likely to be improved by including a more realistic representation of the threshold of motion, and perhaps by accounting for the cover and tools effects.

The main takeaway from our work is that

the saltation– abrasion model, which is the only one that explicitly represents the threshold of motion, predicts a wide range of steady-state topographic slopes that are consistent with field observations and the predictions of other models, and is thus a viable candidate for explaining the evolution of channel networks and the topography of entire landscapes.
the saltation– abrasion model provides a useful reference for evaluating the predictions of other incision models and for interpreting the results of field and laboratory experiments.

the saltation– abrasion incision model, which represents the most important effects of sediment on the incision rate of bedrock rivers and is based on a mechanistic understanding of sediment entrainment, transport and deposition, provides a useful reference for evaluating the ability of alternative incision and landscape evolution models to represent the effects of sediment in controlling the slope of bedrock rivers at the landscape scale.
